title: Inaccessible to Anarchy: the Clerk, the Countess, and the Kingdom Under Asia
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Paris, birth on the rue de l'Échiquier
stops.date_confidence: attested. French Wikipedia gives the date and the exact address, 23 rue de l'Échiquier in the old 3rd arrondissement, and names the father verbatim as physician of the hospitals, internship class of 1833, alienist and physician-in-chief of the house at Charenton. The father's dates 1804-1890 are not verified. A Thèse de Médecine of 1838 attached to the son in one bibliography is four years older than the son and belongs to the father.
stops.campa: In the old third arrondissement, at 23 rue de l'Échiquier, a son is born to Guillaume-Alexandre Saint-Yves, physician of the hospitals, of the internship class of 1833. They name him Joseph Alexandre, eldest of three brothers. The father is an alienist and will become physician-in-chief of the asylum at Charenton, where the state keeps the people it has judged unfit to govern themselves. The son will spend fifty years drawing up a government for everyone else. The street is narrow, given over to printers and engravers, five minutes from the boulevards.
suggested_refs: The house at 23 rue de l'Échiquier, Paris, birthplace given in the civil register

stops.name: Charenton, the house his father governs
stops.date_confidence: mixed. The father's post as alienist and physician-in-chief at Charenton is attested by French Wikipedia. The years of tenure, the son's presence in the household there, and the conflictual, disciplinarian character of the relationship come from Jean Saunier's 1981 biography as relayed by the research dossier and are not independently verified; the dossier itself traces them to the son's later autobiographical writing. The coordinate is the historic Maison de Charenton, today the Esquirol hospital at Saint-Maurice on the Marne. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: The asylum on the Marne is a small state: wards, workshops, a chapel, a garden, and a physician-in-chief whose word inside the walls is not appealed. Guillaume-Alexandre Saint-Yves holds that office. His son grows up as the child of the man who decides who is mad, and describes the household afterward as a discipline rather than a home. Everything he schemes at for the next fifty years turns on one problem, how authority can hold without force behind it. Charenton has the force. It keeps a locked ward and a register of the committed, and the physician-in-chief signs both.
suggested_refs: The Maison nationale de Charenton, now the Hôpital Esquirol, Saint-Maurice
sources: Jean Saunier, Saint-Yves d'Alveydre ou une synarchie sans énigme (1981), via the research dossier

stops.name: Mettray, the colony for the sons of nobody
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was held for a period at the agricultural penal colony for young offenders near Tours, and that its founder made a lasting impression on him: French Wikipedia states both directly. The year, his age, the offence and the legal basis of the detention are unrecovered, so the date orders the segment only. The coordinate is the colony site at Les Bourgetteries, not the commune centre of Mettray, which lies about 850 metres west-northwest.
stops.campa: North of Tours, Frédéric-Auguste Demetz has built a penal colony that looks like a village: no cells, no bars, boys divided into houses of forty under a chef de famille, worked in the fields from dawn, prayed over, drilled, sung to. The adolescent Saint-Yves is sent here after trouble the record does not name. He comes out holding Demetz for the man who turned his life, and never afterward writes about punishment without writing about correction. The houses stand in a semicircle around the chapel; the boys go out to the fields at five in the morning.
suggested_refs: The colonie agricole et pénitentiaire de Mettray, founded 1840 by Frédéric-Auguste Demetz

stops.name: Brest, the naval medical school
stops.date_confidence: attested that his father pushed him toward the service and that he entered the naval medical school at Brest: both Wikipedias name the training. The year is inferred from his age and orders the segment only. The coordinate is the naval hospital, today the Hôpital d'Instruction des Armées Clermont-Tonnerre on the rue Galilée, where the school operated; an earlier coordinate placing him in the arsenal, 1.4 km southwest, was wrong.
stops.campa: His father puts him toward the fleet, and he enters the naval medical school attached to the hospital at Brest, where the navy trains the surgeons it sends around the world. The teaching is dissection, fevers, amputation at sea, the diseases the ships bring back from every latitude. He is not yet of age and the choice is not really his. Of the whole passage nothing survives but the fact of it: no diploma, no register of his classes, no name of a master he studied under, no record of how long he stayed.
suggested_refs: The école de médecine navale at the Brest naval hospital

stops.name: Brest, the black smallpox
stops.date_confidence: attested. French Wikipedia states in its own voice that he volunteered to replace an intern struck by variole noire, contracted it and nearly died, ending the medical training; an earlier note calling this unattested was incorrect. The year is inferred from the 1863 relocation that follows and orders the segment. No medical diploma of his is documented anywhere.
stops.campa: An intern in the hospital falls to variole noire, the black smallpox, the haemorrhagic form that kills inside a week. Saint-Yves volunteers to take his place on the ward, and the ward is where he catches it. He nearly dies of it. When he gets up again the medical career is over: no diploma of his is documented anywhere, and nothing suggests he tried to finish it. He is barely twenty, convalescent, and without a trade to go back to. Nobody wrote down the name of the intern whose place he took on the ward, or whether that man lived.
suggested_refs: The smallpox wards of the Brest naval hospital, early 1860s

stops.name: Saint Helier, the convalescent teaches science
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the island: French Wikipedia gives the 1863 relocation to Jersey and the teaching of science as his means of support, and the 1870 departure. The coordinate is Saint Helier itself; no address of his on the island has been recovered.
stops.campa: Convalescent, without a trade and without money, he crosses to Jersey in 1863 and keeps himself by teaching science to whoever will pay for lessons. The island is small, French-speaking in the country parishes, thick with exiles and their newspapers. He reads: languages, cosmology, the Hebrew alphabet, the histories that claim to reach behind history. Most of what he prints over the next forty years is quarried out of these seven years of unsupervised reading. He arrives a failed naval surgeon at twenty-one and leaves in 1870, when the war starts.
suggested_refs: The French exile press of Saint Helier, 1850s-1860s

stops.name: Havre des Pas, the house Victor Hugo has already left
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved. Both Wikipedias say Saint-Yves was connected on Jersey with Victor Hugo. Hugo's own documented movements put him at Marine Terrace from 16 August 1852 until his expulsion from Jersey on 31 October 1855, after which he lived on Guernsey; Saint-Yves arrives in 1863. No meeting is attested and the chronology does not permit one on the island. The coordinate is the Marine Terrace site at Havre des Pas, used as the landmark the claim points at, not as evidence of a meeting. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Both encyclopedias say that Saint-Yves connected on Jersey with Victor Hugo. The dates refuse it. Hugo was expelled from the island on 31 October 1855 and wrote from Guernsey afterward; Saint-Yves lands in 1863, eight years into that absence, and what he can walk past at Marine Terrace is a house with other tenants in it. The connection, if there is one, is a milieu and a legend rather than a meeting: the same parishes, the same exile newspapers, the same house pointed out to visitors. Neither encyclopedia gives a date for it, or a place, or anybody who saw the two men in a room together.
suggested_refs: Marine Terrace, Havre des Pas, Saint Helier, Hugo's house 1852-1855

stops.name: Jersey, the papers of Fabre d'Olivet
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The introduction through Virginie Faure and the access to Antoine Fabre d'Olivet's legacy and manuscripts appear in the research dossier's synthesis of Léon Cellier and Julian Strube and were not found in either Wikipedia biography or verified against a primary source. That Fabre d'Olivet's system underlies the later books is the settled judgement of the modern scholarship the dossier cites. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Through an acquaintance on the island, Virginie Faure, he comes into the legacy and some of the manuscripts of Antoine Fabre d'Olivet, dead since 1825: the restored Hebrew tongue, the primordial language standing behind all languages, a sacred prehistory of the race running back before any archive. Saint-Yves takes the whole apparatus, and takes it without much acknowledgement. Every book of the Missions will stand on it, and in twenty years a reviewer will say so in print. How the introduction was made, and what Virginie Faure was to either man, is in none of the sources; her name is the whole of what survives of her.
suggested_refs: Antoine Fabre d'Olivet, La Langue hébraïque restituée (1815-1816) and Histoire philosophique du genre humain (1824)
sources: Research dossier, synthesizing Léon Cellier and Julian Strube; not independently verified

stops.name: Paris, the marine infantry and the wound
stops.date_confidence: attested in part. Both Wikipedias state that he returned to France in 1870, enlisted in the marine infantry and was wounded during reconnaissance operations. The 171st marching battalion and the fort before which he is said to have fallen appear in neither, and French bataillons de marche of 1870-71 were not numbered that high; both details are dropped as unsupported. The coordinate is a placeholder for Paris: no action, unit or ground could be identified. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: War with Prussia calls him back across the Channel in 1870, and he enlists in the marine infantry, the naval troops thrown into the land defence of a country losing its army faster than it can count them. He is wounded on a reconnaissance. Which reconnaissance, on what ground, before which works, the record does not say; the battalion number and the fort that circulate in later accounts are in no source that can be checked. He is twenty-eight. This is the only fighting of his life.
suggested_refs: The marine infantry in the land defence of France, 1870-1871

stops.name: Place Beauvau, seven years as a clerk
stops.date_confidence: attested that he worked as a commis at the Ministry of the Interior from after the war until 1878: both Wikipedias give the employment and the terminal year. The Place Beauvau coordinate is the ministry's historic seat; his own office is not identified.
stops.campa: After the siege and the Commune he takes a clerk's post at the Ministry of the Interior and keeps it until 1878: registers, circulars, the correspondence of prefects, the machinery of a Republic three years old and not yet sure that it will last. Seven years of it, from the age of twenty-nine. He is copying out the administration of France by day and writing about the government of the world by night. What his colleagues at Beauvau made of the second occupation is not recorded; his own office there has never been identified. The first books he publishes come out while he is still on its rolls, drawing the salary.
suggested_refs: The Ministry of the Interior at the Place Beauvau, Paris

stops.name: Paris, two books from the same publisher
stops.date_confidence: attested for the two 1877 books: the BnF catalogue holds Testament lyrique and Les Clefs de l'Orient, both Didier, Paris, 1877. Le Retour du Christ, dated 1874 in every bibliography that copies the previous bibliography, was not found in the BnF catalogue under his name and stays unverified. The contents of Les Clefs de l'Orient are reported from the dossier's summary of the Wikipedia chronology. The coordinate is a Paris placeholder; his residence in these years is not fixed.
stops.campa: Didier brings out two of his books in a single year. Testament lyrique is verse. Les Clefs de l'Orient takes birth, sex, love and death together with what he calls the Eastern Cabala, and proposes to settle the Eastern Question by reconciling the three religions that claim the same scriptures. A third title, Le Retour du Christ, is credited to him in 1874 by every list that copies the list before it, and no catalogue consulted holds a copy of it; whether it was ever printed nobody has established. He is thirty-five, and a clerk at the Ministry of the Interior.
suggested_refs: Les Clefs de l'Orient (Paris, Didier, 1877), BnF catalogue record
sources: BnF catalogue général (Testament lyrique; Clefs de l'Orient, Didier, 1877)
WebFetch summary of the Wikipedia chronology

stops.name: Mecca, the qibla he never travels to
stops.date_confidence: thematic pin, not a journey. There is no evidence that Saint-Yves ever traveled outside France, Jersey, Britain and San Marino, and none that he went to Arabia; the documented geography of his life is entirely European. Les Clefs de l'Orient (Didier, Paris, 1877) is attested by the BnF catalogue; its proposal of a Jewish, Christian and Muslim settlement is reported from the dossier's summary and is not independently verified. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: The settlement he proposes in Les Clefs de l'Orient runs through three cities he will never see. Paris, Tours, Brest, Jersey: that is the whole of his geography so far, and Arabia is not in it. He writes about the House at Mecca as a term in an equation, one third of a reconciliation to be arranged between scriptures by a French clerk at a desk on the Place Beauvau. While he writes, the Eastern Question is being settled in the Balkans by Russian and Ottoman armies who have not read him.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram, term of the reconciliation proposed in Les Clefs de l'Orient
sources: BnF catalogue général (Clefs de l'Orient, Didier, 1877)

stops.name: Westminster, the marriage that ends the clerkship
stops.date_confidence: date and bride attested, venue not. French Wikipedia gives 6 September 1877 and Marie Victoire de Riznitch Rzewuska (1827-1895), a relative of Madame Hanska; English Wikipedia calls her a relative of Honoré de Balzac. Westminster and London are in neither and rest on the dossier alone, so the place is a reconstruction; her birth at Odessa is likewise unverified. Russian Wikipedia gives her first husband as Count Eduard Fyodorovich Keller (1819-1903), senator and privy councillor, so the first marriage ended by divorce or annulment and she is not a widow. The precise genealogy, that her mother Polina Adamovna Rzewuska was a sister of Ewelina Hanska, is dossier-only and unconfirmed.
stops.campa: On 6 September 1877 he marries Marie Victoire de Riznitch Rzewuska, Countess Keller, fifteen years his senior, out of the Rzewuski connection that gave Honoré de Balzac the wife he courted for seventeen years. Her first husband, Count Eduard Fyodorovich Keller, senator and privy councillor, is alive and will outlive them both; this marriage ends by law and not by death. Her fortune is large. In 1878 Saint-Yves walks out of the Ministry of the Interior and never works for a salary again.
suggested_refs: Alexandre Cabanel, Portrait de la comtesse de Keller (1873), now Musée d'Orsay, Paris
sources: honore_de_balzac.journey.json (the Hanska courtship and the 1850 marriage)

stops.name: Paris, a tragedy in five acts and a study of seaweed
stops.date_confidence: attested for both books. The BnF catalogue holds Mystère du progrès: tragédie historique en 5 actes, avec choeurs et ballets (Didier, Paris, 1878), the five acts, choruses and ballets being the catalogue's own words; the Wikipedia chronology gives De l'utilité des algues marines (1879) and the failure of the venture for want of capital. The month orders the two years as one stop.
stops.campa: Freed from the ministry, he publishes within two years a historical tragedy in five acts with choruses and ballets, called Mystère du progrès, and a technical argument for the industrial exploitation of marine algae. The first is addressed to the shape of history; the second wants a factory. He is trying in these years to be several men at once. Neither book finds its public, the algae venture fails for want of capital, and the capital in all of it was his wife's.
suggested_refs: Mystère du progrès (Paris, Didier, 1878); De l'utilité des algues marines (1879)
sources: BnF catalogue général (Mystère du progrès, Didier, 1878)
WebFetch summary of the Wikipedia chronology (algues marines, 1879)

stops.name: San Marino, the marquisate
stops.date_confidence: attested that San Marino conferred the title Marquis d'Alveydre in 1880 and that he used the name thereafter: both Wikipedias give it. Contradiction flagged and not resolved: one account has the title granted, another has it sold in conjunction with an Italian property purchase, and a further claim that the Vatican conferred it conflicts with the better-sourced San Marino account. No decree has been located. The estate near the Franco-Italian border from which the name is said to derive appears only in the dossier and has never been located; the coordinate here is the city of San Marino, inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: The smallest republic in Europe, on its rock above Rimini, makes him Marquis d'Alveydre in 1880. Whether the title is granted for his writings or sold alongside an Italian property is exactly the thing the surviving accounts do not agree on, and no decree has been produced by anybody. A rival version has it from the Vatican, which the better sources do not support. The name is said to come from an estate his wife buys near the Franco-Italian border, and nobody has found the estate. From this year he signs every book Saint-Yves d'Alveydre.
suggested_refs: The archives of the Republic of San Marino, sought for a decree of 1880 and not located

stops.name: Brussels, synarchy read out at the peace congress
stops.date_confidence: attested for the event: French Wikipedia states that he delivered a lecture on synarchy at the international peace congress at Brussels in October 1882. The congress's full name, given elsewhere as the International Congress of Arbitration and Federation of Peace, and the affiliation with the Union de la Paix sociale associated with Frédéric Le Play, are dossier-only and unverified. The coordinate is the Grand-Place as a central-city landmark; the hall is not identified. An earlier coordinate for this stop fell in rural Champagne, 220 km from Brussels, and is corrected here.
stops.campa: In October 1882 he stands up at the international peace congress in Brussels and reads out synarchy: not a party, not a revolution, but three chambers standing above politics, for teaching, for justice and for economy, each composed of the people who actually do the work. Government by profession rather than by majority. He is not a secret society and does not claim to be one. What stands behind him is his wife's money and a printer, and he says the whole thing out loud, from a platform, to a room of delegates who had come to discuss arbitration between states. Which hall, and how they took it, the proceedings would say; nobody has read them.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the Brussels international peace congress, October 1882

stops.name: Paris, the two Missions of 1882
stops.date_confidence: attested. The French Wikipedia chronology and the WebFetch Wikipedia summary both give Mission des souverains (Mission actuelle des souverains) and Mission des ouvriers (Mission actuelle des ouvriers) in 1882; archive.org holds Mission actuelle des souverains, E. Dentu, 1882. The coordinate is a Paris placeholder.
stops.campa: Mission actuelle des souverains goes to the crowned heads of Europe: a history of Christian government and a plan for a synarchic Europe, addressed to the men who could enact it by decree. Mission actuelle des ouvriers goes to the workers, and tells them to organize by trade and by profession outside every political party, which is not what the party of order wants to hear and not what the party of revolution wants to hear either. The two are printed in the same year, addressed to the top of Europe and the bottom of it, and he expects them to meet somewhere in between. E. Dentu of Paris prints them both.
suggested_refs: Mission actuelle des souverains (Paris, E. Dentu, 1882), digitized at archive.org
sources: WebFetch summary of the Wikipedia chronology

stops.name: Paris, Mission des Juifs
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book: the BnF catalogue gives Mission des Juifs, Calmann Lévy, Paris, 1884, and archive.org holds a scanned 1884 copy. The claim that it draws heavily and inadequately attributedly on Fabre d'Olivet is the judgement of modern scholarship as reported in the WebFetch Wikipedia summary and the dossier's account of Strube after Cellier; the figure of seventy-four centuries is Saint-Yves's own.
stops.campa: Calmann Lévy publishes it in 1884: a sacred history of what he calls the seventy-four centuries before Christianity, in which Israel carries a providential mission for the whole race and the constitution of Moses is the model every later government has fallen away from. It is the largest of his books and the one that makes his name in the occult reviews. Nearly all of its prehistory comes from Fabre d'Olivet, dead fifty-nine years. Cellier said so, and Strube after him. The book does not.
suggested_refs: Mission des Juifs (Paris, Calmann Lévy, 1884), digitized at archive.org

stops.name: Temple Mount, the mission assigned from a desk in Paris
stops.date_confidence: thematic pin, not a journey: no evidence exists that Saint-Yves ever traveled to Jerusalem or anywhere in the Levant, and the dossier states the gap itself. The pin marks the subject of Mission des Juifs (BnF: Calmann Lévy, 1884), whose providential reading of Israel's history is attested as the book's content; the interpretation of the Mosaic constitution as his political model is his own argument as summarized in the sources. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: The centre of the history he writes is a hill he has never stood on. Moses, the priesthood, the double temple, a covenant mislaid and to be recovered: he assigns a people and a rock a mission spanning seventy-four centuries, and does it out of French translations and a dead man's manuscripts, without leaving France. He never goes to Jerusalem and never proposes to go. In his account the place is not a place at all but a constitutional precedent, the last time on earth that authority was arranged the right way round.
suggested_refs: Mission des Juifs (1884), its reading of the Mosaic constitution
sources: BnF catalogue général (Mission des Juifs, Calmann Lévy, 1884)
Research dossier (the gap: no evidence of travel to India, Tibet, Central Asia or the Levant)

stops.name: Paris, the charge of theft
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the review, attested for the answer. The 1885 review by Victor Meunier accusing him of plagiarizing Fabre d'Olivet comes from the dossier's synthesis of Julian Strube and Léon Cellier; the original text was not located, and Gallica's full-text search refused the requests made to it. The quoted sentence is verbatim from the Inner Traditions translation of Mission de l'Inde en Europe, printed in 1886, a year after the charge; the identification of the august departed individual as Fabre d'Olivet is the reading of the modern scholarship, not Saint-Yves's own words.
stops.campa: A review by Victor Meunier accuses him of lifting Mission des Juifs out of Fabre d'Olivet. Modern scholarship, Cellier and after him Strube, largely sustains the borrowing while dividing over how much of synarchy itself is his. His answer is printed a year later, in the book he then destroys, and it names its source by refusing to name him. Not from any living initiate of Asia, he writes, but from an august departed individual about whom he has already spoken in Mission of the Jews.
stops.quote: I do not owe my Synarchic enlightenment about the past and about the present to any Asiatic initiate currently living, but to several clues vouchsafed me by an august departed individual about whom I have spoken in Mission of the Jews.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, Mission de l'Inde en Europe (1886), trans. Jon E. Graham as The Kingdom of Agarttha, Inner Traditions, 2008; archive.org full text, lines 1458-1460
suggested_refs: Julian Strube on Saint-Yves and Fabre d'Olivet; Léon Cellier, Fabre d'Olivet (1953)
sources: Research dossier, citing Strube and Cellier
The Kingdom of Agarttha, Inner Traditions ed., archive.org full text

stops.name: Paris, the funerals of Victor Hugo
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book: the BnF catalogue holds Les Funérailles de Victor Hugo, par l'auteur des Missions, signed Saint-Yves-d'Alveydre, impr. de A. Lahure, Paris, 1885. Hugo died on 22 May 1885 and was buried on 1 June, so the imprint is coherent. Whether Saint-Yves was himself in the crowd on 1 June is not attested; the coordinate is a Paris placeholder and the date is the day of the funeral, not a documented sighting of him at it.
stops.campa: Hugo dies on 22 May 1885 and is carried to the Panthéon on the first of June behind a crowd Paris has never matched. Twenty-two years earlier Saint-Yves had crossed to Jersey and found the great exile already eight years gone from the island. Now he writes a book about the funeral, printed by Lahure the same year, and signs it not Saint-Yves d'Alveydre but par l'auteur des Missions, by the author of the Missions. Whether he was in the street that day nobody says. The catafalque had stood under the Arc de Triomphe all the night before.
suggested_refs: Les Funérailles de Victor Hugo, par l'auteur des Missions (Paris, impr. A. Lahure, 1885)

segments.name: Agarttha, and the Book He Burned

stops.name: Levallois-Perret, the Sanskrit teacher
stops.date_confidence: mixed, with a source contradiction flagged. English Wikipedia's Agartha article attests that he was introduced to the idea of Agartha by a man named Haji Sharif or Hardjji Scharipf who taught him Sanskrit and whose origins are largely unknown. The exact date of 8 June 1885, the address at 108 rue de Cormeille in Levallois-Perret, and the lesson heading naming guru Pandit H. S. Bagwandass of the Great Agartthian School rest solely on Joscelyn Godwin's study of Sorbonne MS 1824 as reported by the dossier; the manuscript could not be reached, nubis.univ-paris1.fr now redirecting to nubis.bis-sorbonne.fr, the ark returning 404 and Calames timing out. Contradiction: English Wikipedia's biography article frames 1885 instead as a visit from a group of Eastern Initiates, one named Prince Hardjij Scharipf, not as paid lessons. The coordinate is the town centre of Levallois-Perret.
stops.campa: A man in Levallois-Perret calling himself Haji Sharif, or Hardjji Scharipf, whose origins nobody has ever established, begins teaching him Sanskrit in 1885. The surviving lesson papers are said to run under the heading of a guru of the Great Agartthian School. Whether Saint-Yves is a paying pupil of an obscure teacher in a suburb or the chosen recipient of a delegation of Eastern initiates depends entirely on which account is read, and the two stand side by side with neither withdrawn. He swears nothing to anybody, and says so in print.
stops.quote: Nevertheless, as a spontaneous initiate, I have never at any time in my life given any teaching body, nor any individual, any manner of oath pledging not to reveal whatever I might learn or grasp in order to do good to my fellow humans.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, Mission de l'Inde en Europe (1886), trans. as The Kingdom of Agarttha, Inner Traditions, 2008; archive.org full text, lines 1439-1441
suggested_refs: Bibliothèque interuniversitaire de la Sorbonne, MS 1824, the Sanskrit lesson papers, studied by Joscelyn Godwin; not reachable online at the time of writing
sources: Research dossier, reporting Godwin on Sorbonne MS 1824

stops.name: Paris, the alphabet called Vattanian
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Vattanian language which Sharif presented as the tongue of Agartha was Sharif's own invention: English Wikipedia states it. That the alphabet becomes the foundation of the later Archéomètre is the settled account of his final work in French Wikipedia. The coordinate is 27 rue Vernet in the 8th arrondissement, the residence where the dossier places the household in these years and to which a Christmas letter from Sharif is said to be addressed; the address itself is dossier-only and unverified, though the street coordinate is confirmed. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Sharif gives him a language. Vattan, or Vattanian, is presented as the original speech of Agarttha, the tongue from which Hebrew and Sanskrit descend, its letters keys to number, sound and colour at once. Saint-Yves builds on it for the rest of his life, and the Archéomètre is its instrument. Later examination of the material concludes that the teacher made it up. Saint-Yves copies the letters out, learns them, and is still working on their correspondences of number, sound and colour twenty-three years later, in the last winter of his life.
suggested_refs: The Vattanian alphabet as reproduced in L'Archéomètre (Paris, Dorbon-Aîné)

stops.name: Paris, Mission de l'Inde privately printed
stops.date_confidence: attested that he privately printed the book in 1886: English Wikipedia's Agartha article gives the printing and the near-total destruction that followed. The month is arbitrary and orders the segment. The quoted sentence is verbatim from the Inner Traditions translation, read directly in the archive.org full text.
stops.campa: In 1886 he has printed, at his own charge and not for sale, Mission de l'Inde en Europe, Mission de l'Europe en Asie: the question of the Mahatma and its solution. It reports, in the flat voice of a geographer, a kingdom under the surface of Asia, governed synarchically, with universities, an archive of the whole race, and a pontiff nobody sees. He does not offer it as a vision or a romance. He offers it as intelligence, gathered by means he declines to specify, about a government currently in session.
stops.quote: The sacred territory of Agarttha is independent, organized in accordance with Synarchic principles, and consists of a population that has grown to approach twenty million souls.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, The Kingdom of Agarttha, Inner Traditions ed.; archive.org full text, lines 1579-1581
suggested_refs: Mission de l'Inde en Europe (1886), of which two copies survived the recall
sources: The Kingdom of Agarttha, Inner Traditions ed., archive.org full text

stops.name: Paris, the name that means inaccessible to violence
stops.date_confidence: attested as text, with an OCR caveat. The English rendering, that the name means inaccessible to violence and inaccessible to Anarchy, was read directly in the Inner Traditions full text. The French line as printed in the 1910 Dorbon-Aîné edition carries two OCR artifacts in the archive.org scan: a garbled hierogram plus the verb signifie, and a marginal gloss, mystique, bleeding into the line; only the clean flanking fragment is quoted here. The 1910 text prints l'anarchie lowercase in this line and capitalized elsewhere. The coordinate is the rue Vernet residence, dossier-only; the day orders the segment.
stops.campa: The word is glossed at its first appearance, and the gloss is the whole doctrine folded into one line: Agarttha means ungraspable by violence, inaccessible to anarchy. He has spent four years writing against anarchy, which for him is not the bombs but the condition of a society whose authority has no root. Synarchy is its opposite, and the kingdom under Asia is synarchy that was kept when everyone above ground lost it. The gloss sits in the margin of the page on which the word first appears, in the printer's small type, beside a hierogram of his own devising.
stops.quote: insaisissable à la violence, inaccessible à l'anarchie.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, Mission de l'Inde en Europe, 1910 Dorbon-Aîné edition; archive.org identifier missiondelindeeneurope, _djvu.txt at offset 36367

stops.name: Paris, the kingdom without prisons
stops.date_confidence: attested as text: both sentences are verbatim from the Inner Traditions translation, read directly in the archive.org full text at lines 1595-1596 and 1598. The juxtaposition with Mettray and Charenton is the reading of this file, not a claim made anywhere by Saint-Yves; the Mettray detention is attested by French Wikipedia, the father's Charenton post likewise. The day orders the segment.
stops.campa: Of everything he reports about Agarttha, what he sets down early is the penal law: there are no prisons there, and the death penalty is not applied. The man writing it was sent as a boy to an agricultural penal colony for young offenders and came out grateful to its founder, and grew up in the household of the physician who governed the asylum at Charenton. He is forty-four when he writes the penal chapters, and he designs a country in which nobody is confined at all. He does not mention Mettray in them, or Charenton, or his father.
stops.quote: None of our frightful judicial or penitentiary systems are known in Agarttha: there are no prisons.

stops.name: Paris, the pontiff on the white elephant
stops.date_confidence: attested as text: the triangle of Brahatmah, Mahatma and Mahanga is quoted from the Inner Traditions translation at lines 1881-1884, where the OCR renders the Sanskrit script as unreadable symbols but the English prose is clean; the elephant passage is at lines 3213-3214 and the statement that nobody outside the highest initiates has seen the pontiff at lines 3207-3208. Saint-Yves's assertion that the reigning Brahatmah took the throne in 1848 was seen only in part and is not carried here. The day orders the segment.
stops.campa: At the head of the hidden government stands a triangle: the Brahatmah, support of souls in the mind of God, with the Mahatma for the universal soul and the Mahanga for the body of the cosmos. Below them the degrees of initiates run into the tens of thousands. Nobody outside the highest degree has ever seen the pontiff's face. When he does appear he appears mounted, and the light coming off him is described the way a man describes a thing he has been told about carefully and at length.
stops.quote: Mounted on his white elephant, he is all awash from his tiara to his feet in a dazzling light that blinds all eyes, with similar sparkling lights surrounding him.

stops.name: Paris, the edition recalled and destroyed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the act, contradictory for the motive. English Wikipedia's Agartha article gives the recall and destruction of nearly the whole edition within about a fortnight, one copy kept by the author and one secretly retained by the printer. The competing explanations, that his masters forbade the disclosure and that Indian informants threatened him, are both in that article; the specific attribution to Jules Bois and the specific charge of threatened litigation over unauthorized publication are dossier-only and could not be located. The judgement that the later assassination legends are embellishment is a characterization, not a sourced finding. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Within about a fortnight of the printing he recalls the whole edition and destroys it. He keeps one copy. The printer, without telling him, keeps another, and those two are all that survive. The reasons given do not agree: that his masters forbade the publication of what he had let out, that the man who supplied the material threatened him at law over it, that Indians threatened his life, which is the version that grew afterward and rests on nothing anyone has produced. He never explains it in print himself.
stops.quote: But nowhere will there be found among them a traitor who would provide the precise location where its Council of God and its Council of Gods, its pontifical head and its judicial heart, are located.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, The Kingdom of Agarttha, Inner Traditions ed.; archive.org full text, lines 1531-1533

stops.name: Paris, La France vraie
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book and its purpose: the WebFetch summary of the Wikipedia chronology gives La France vraie in 1887, including autobiographical material written partly to rebut the accusations of plagiarism and to defend the originality of synarchy. Vœux du Syndicat de la presse économique, also dated 1887 in the dossier's bibliography, was not verified against a catalogue and is not given a stop.
stops.campa: He writes it partly to answer the accusation. Into a book about the true France he folds his own life, the island years, the reading, the descent of the doctrine, arguing that synarchy is his own and that whatever came from Fabre d'Olivet came to him as it comes to an heir. It is the nearest thing to an autobiography he leaves behind, and it was written under attack, which is a condition that improves nobody's memory. No copy of it has been confirmed online, and the review it answers has not been found either.
suggested_refs: La France vraie (1887), the autobiographical passages
sources: WebFetch summary of the Wikipedia chronology

stops.name: Paris, the warning about a blond Russian
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The somnambulistic consultation of 17 June 1887 and its warning that his wife would be assassinated by a blond Russian within eighteen months to two years appear only in the dossier's citation of Saint-Yves's own notes; the note itself was not located and is in neither Wikipedia biography. The coordinate is the rue Vernet residence, itself dossier-only; the consultation's location is not recorded. That no such assassination occurred and that Marie Victoire died in 1895 are secure.
stops.campa: On 17 June 1887 a somnambulist consulted in trance tells him to guard his wife: within eighteen months to two years she will be killed by a blond Russian. He writes it down and keeps the paper. She is a Russian countess whose first husband is a senator of the Empire and still alive, so the warning has an address to go to. Nothing happens. Marie Victoire dies eight years later, of nothing anyone has called violence. He kept the paper all the same, and it is on the strength of that paper alone that any of this is known; why a man files a prophecy that failed is not a question the record answers.
suggested_refs: Saint-Yves's own notes on the consultation of 17 June 1887, cited in the research dossier and not located

stops.name: Paris, the banquet of the Syndicat
stops.date_confidence: attested in part. The BnF catalogue holds Les États-généraux du suffrage universel: discours prononcé au banquet du Syndicat de la presse économique, published in 1888 au siège du Syndicat, Paris, which fixes the body as real, Paris-based, holding banquets he addressed. The 1886 founding year, his role as founder, the fuller name et professionnelle de France, and the campaign for a Conseil de l'économie nationale addressed with Baron Théodore de Cambourg to Presidents Jules Grévy and Sadi Carnot are all dossier-only and unverified. The coordinate is a Paris placeholder; the Syndicat's premises are not located. Reordered after the 1887 stops so the segment runs chronologically.
stops.campa: He speaks at the banquet of the Syndicat de la presse économique, whose premises are somewhere in Paris and whose printed proceedings survive; the speech is called The Estates-General of Universal Suffrage. This is the aboveground half of the doctrine that went underground in the other book: professional chambers, an economic council of the nation, petitions carried to the President of the Republic. Universal suffrage as practised counts heads. He wants it to count trades. No article of the constitution is altered as a result.
suggested_refs: Les États-généraux du suffrage universel (Paris, au siège du Syndicat, 1888), BnF catalogue record

stops.name: Paris, the poem for Queen Victoria
stops.date_confidence: attested for both books. The BnF catalogue holds Le Poème de la reine, dédié à S. M. la reine d'Angleterre, A. Lahure, Paris, 1889, and The poem of the Queen Victoria, by the Earl of Lytton, translated into English verses from le Poème de la Reine, A. Lahure, Paris, 1892, printed by the same house in Paris rather than in London. Robert Bulwer-Lytton, 1st Earl of Lytton, died in November 1891, so the issue is posthumous for the translator. The structure of twenty-two stanzas keyed to the Hebrew alphabet is in no catalogue record and stays a reconstruction.
stops.campa: Lahure prints Le Poème de la Reine in 1889, dedicated to Her Majesty the Queen of England, its stanzas said to run to twenty-two, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Robert Bulwer-Lytton, Earl of Lytton, puts it into English verse. Lytton dies in November 1891; the translation comes out in 1892, from the same Paris printer, after him. What the Queen made of a marquis of San Marino counting out her praises in the letters of the Hebrew alphabet is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The poem of the Queen Victoria, trans. the Earl of Lytton (Paris, A. Lahure, 1892)

stops.name: Paris, Jeanne d'Arc victorieuse
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book: the BnF catalogue gives Jeanne d'Arc victorieuse, épopée nationale, dédiée à l'armée française, L. Sauvaitre, Paris, 1890, the dedication in the catalogue's own words. The content of the preface, and specifically the announced end of active synarchic campaigning, is dossier-only; the preface could not be read. That he undertook no further political campaign is consistent with the record but is not itself attested.
stops.campa: Sauvaitre publishes the national epic in 1890, dedicated to the French army. He is forty-eight. In the preface, according to the accounts, he declares that he is done campaigning for synarchy: the Missions are written, the sovereigns have not answered, the workers have not organized by trade, the Republic has convened no economic council. Nineteen years of work remain to him and none of it will be political. The maid of Domrémy is the last public subject he takes up.
suggested_refs: Jeanne d'Arc victorieuse, épopée nationale (Paris, L. Sauvaitre, 1890)

stops.name: Versailles, the house on the rue Colbert
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The move in 1893 from an hôtel particulier at 27 rue Vernet in the 8th arrondissement to a house at 9 rue Colbert in Versailles is dossier-only and in neither Wikipedia biography; the financial pressure said to have caused it is likewise unverified. The street coordinate is confirmed for rue Colbert in the Notre-Dame quarter of Versailles; the house number is not. Note that the rue Vernet has borne that name since 1864, for the Vernet family of painters collectively, and was never called rue Horace-Vernet.
stops.campa: The fortune has been spent: on printing, on the seaweed, on the marquisate, on a household in an hôtel particulier at 27 rue Vernet in the eighth arrondissement. He is fifty-one, and the move that follows is a retrenchment: out of the quarter of the new money, into a provincial town that has been living off an empty palace for a hundred years. In 1893 they take a house at 9 rue Colbert in Versailles, in the Notre-Dame quarter, a few streets from the château.

stops.name: Paris, chevalier of the Légion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: attested for the decoration: French Wikipedia states that he was made chevalier of the Légion d'honneur in 1893. The ceremony site is unrecovered and the coordinate is a Paris placeholder; the month orders the segment. The Léonore file that would carry the citation could not be consulted: the database is a JavaScript application that returns only a page title to fetching, and its POP API mirror returned 403. Reading the honour as official encouragement is interpretation, not a sourced finding.
stops.campa: The Republic makes him a chevalier in 1893. It has adopted no line of his constitution, will convene no economic council, and has left the Missions to the occult reviews; it gives him the cross anyway, as it gives it to men of letters who have written a great deal and troubled nobody. His admirers read the ribbon as encouragement. The citation that would say what the Republic thought it was rewarding sits in the Légion d'honneur files, unopened by anyone who has written about him. He is fifty-one, and this is the only thing the French state ever gives him.
suggested_refs: Base Léonore, the Légion d'honneur dossier for Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, not consulted

stops.name: Versailles, the death of Marie Victoire
stops.date_confidence: year attested, setting reconstructed. French Wikipedia gives her dates as 1827-1895, from which the age of sixty-seven or sixty-eight follows arithmetically. Death at Versailles, in the rue Colbert house, at about one in the morning, is dossier-only; French Wikipedia gives no place of death for her. His subsequent withdrawal from public politics is also a reconstruction. The month is not established and orders the segment.
stops.campa: She dies in 1895, sixty-seven or sixty-eight years old, eighteen years married to him. She had been his fortune, his access and his household, and in the accounts of the Sanskrit lessons she is sometimes another pupil in the room. After her the political campaign is finished in fact as well as in a preface: no more petitions, no more addresses to presidents, no more banquets of the economic press. He is fifty-three. He stays on in the rue Colbert house for another fourteen years and does not marry again.
suggested_refs: The shared tomb at the Cimetière Notre-Dame, Versailles, where she is laid in 1895

stops.name: Paris, the sacred music printed on sheets
stops.date_confidence: attested through the BnF catalogue, which holds the run of sheets printed by imp. Delanchy between 1900 and 1902: Salutation angélique in Latin and in Slavonic, Kyrie eleison in Greek, Pater noster, Amrita, L'Étoile des Mages, Isola Bella. Whether any of them has been digitized is not established. The reading of them as archeometry set to intervals follows his own later musical titles and is inference, not a sourced statement. The date orders the run as one stop.
stops.campa: Between 1900 and 1902 the printer Delanchy issues a run of small musical settings: the angelic salutation in Latin and again in Slavonic, a Kyrie eleison in Greek, a Pater noster, and pieces called Amrita, L'Étoile des Mages, Isola Bella. They are the archeometric system heard rather than seen, the same correspondences of letter, number and colour set out as intervals. A widower in a Versailles house is scoring the Ave Maria in Church Slavonic and paying to have it engraved.

stops.name: Paris, taken up by Papus
stops.date_confidence: attested. The BnF holds Notes sur la tradition cabalistique, édition de l'Initiation, Paris, 1901, and separately Papus, La Cabbale: tradition secrète de l'Occident, ouvrage précédé d'une Lettre d'Ad. Franck et d'une Étude par Saint-Yves, Bibliothèque Chacornac, Paris, 1903, whose contents list includes Notes sur la tradition cabalistique. The carrying volume is therefore 1903, not 1901, and the dossier's dating of the Papus link to 1901 is corrected here. That Saint-Yves never joined an order is consistent with his own printed statement that he swore no oath to any teaching body. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He prints Notes sur la tradition cabalistique with the press of L'Initiation in 1901, and two years later Gérard Encausse, who signs himself Papus and runs the Martinist Order out of Paris, carries it into his own La Cabbale beside a letter of Adolphe Franck. Saint-Yves takes no degree and joins no order. The young occultists of Paris treat him as a master anyway. He is fifty-nine and six years a widower, and it is Papus who prints him now and Papus who will decide, after his death, which of the papers become a book.
suggested_refs: Papus, La Cabbale: tradition secrète de l'Occident (Paris, Bibliothèque Chacornac, 1903)

stops.name: Versailles, the instrument that stays on paper
stops.date_confidence: mixed. Diatonie archéométrique: les heptacordes, conjugaisons modales binaires (1907) and L'Archéomètre musical: modes mélodiques et harmoniques (1909) come from the dossier's bibliography and were not verified against a catalogue individually, though the BnF holds musical works of his from these years. The patent applications from 1903 for archeometric applications, chiefly musical, are dossier-only, with no patent numbers or legal disposition recovered; that no instrument was manufactured and no patent earned money is a negative finding, not a document. The date covers the run of years as one stop.
stops.campa: From 1903 he files patent applications on archeometric applications, most of them musical. Diatonie archéométrique: les heptacordes follows in 1907 and L'Archéomètre musical in 1909, thin technical pamphlets written as the working manual of a device that would fix letter, note, number, planet and colour on a single dial. No instrument is ever manufactured and no patent ever earns anything. The great compiled book is not finished. He is sixty-seven years old.

segments.name: Pau, and What Came Up After

stops.name: Pau, the last winter
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the place: French and English Wikipedia both give death at Pau on 5 February 1909. The medical cause is not documented in any source consulted. The therapeutic motive is dossier-only, and the dossier's description of Pau as a thermal-cure district is wrong: Pau has no springs, and was a climatic winter station, the Pyrenean thermal stations being Eaux-Bonnes and Eaux-Chaudes nearby.
stops.campa: He dies at Pau on 5 February 1909, sixty-six years old. Pau is not a spa town and has no springs. It is the climatic station of the Pyrenean foothills, where mild air and an English colony had been drawing the consumptive and the failing since the middle of the century, and the failing came in winter. What he died of is recorded nowhere that has been consulted, nor whether he went south to be cured or simply to be somewhere warm at the end. It is seven hundred kilometres from the house at Versailles where he had spent the last fourteen years.
suggested_refs: Pau as a climatic winter station of the Pyrenean foothills

stops.name: Versailles, the tomb at the Cimetière Notre-Dame
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial: French Wikipedia gives burial at the cimetière Notre-Dame at Versailles in the tomb shared with his wife, and illustrates the article with a photograph of the grave captioned la tombe du Marquis de Saint-Yves. The exact day of the funeral is unknown and orders the segment. The division, plot number and full inscription could not be checked: landrucimetieres.fr and findagrave.com both returned 403. The coordinate is the cemetery itself; an earlier figure placed it 1.1 km south, in open ground.
stops.campa: He is buried in February at the Cimetière Notre-Dame in Versailles, in the tomb where his wife has lain since 1895. A photograph of the stone taken a century later carries the caption the tomb of the Marquis de Saint-Yves, the San Marino title outlasting both the man and the doctrine. Which division, which plot, and what the inscription says in full remain unestablished. The two of them are in one grave in a provincial cemetery, a short walk from the rue Colbert, in a town he came to late and did not choose.

stops.name: Paris, the buried book comes up
stops.date_confidence: attested. English Wikipedia's Agartha article gives the 1910 publication of Mission de l'Inde en Europe, the destroyed 1886 edition having survived in two known copies; French Wikipedia adds that the copy which made it possible reached Papus by way of Count Keller. The month is unknown and orders the segment.
stops.campa: In 1910 Mission de l'Inde en Europe is published for the public for the first time, twenty-four years after he burned it. The copy that makes it possible reaches Papus by way of Count Keller, the family of his wife's first husband, which is a route nobody could have designed. Everything the century that follows does with Agartha comes downstream of this printing. Two copies survived the recall: his own, and the one the printer had kept without telling him.
stops.quote: In Asia alone there are a half a billion people who are more or less aware of its existence and its greatness—not to mention America, whose subterranean regions belonged to Agarttha in very remote antiquity.
stops.quote_source: Saint-Yves d'Alveydre, The Kingdom of Agarttha, Inner Traditions ed.; archive.org full text, lines 1527-1529

stops.name: Paris, the Archéomètre assembled by other hands
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged, not resolved. French Wikipedia dates the posthumous L'Archéomètre to 1910. The archive.org copy, identifier archeometre, is catalogued Dorbon-Aîné, Paris, 1911, while the item's own note says the book appeared l'année suivante after his 1909 death, contradicting its own date field. The BnF holds a Dorbon aîné printing carrying no date at all, plus a second edition preceded by a study by Papus. The editorship of Gérard Encausse and collaborators is confirmed by the archive.org item text. The month orders the segment and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: Papus and a group of friends and collaborators gather the diagrams, the plates, the notebooks and the technical fragments and publish them as one thick volume, L'Archéomètre, key to all the religions and all the sciences of antiquity, from Dorbon-Aîné in Paris. The book he could not finish exists, in an edition he did not make and was not alive to correct. Whether the year on it is 1910 or 1911 the sources refuse to agree, and one printing of it carries no date at all.
suggested_refs: L'Archéomètre (Paris, Dorbon-Aîné), digitized at archive.org as archeometre

stops.name: Paris, the notebooks at the Sorbonne
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, from a single archival record. The NuBIS record for MS 1823/5, Cahier de notes I: notes sur l'existence historique de Jésus, 303 leaves, gives the manuscript as a gift of Papus to the Bibliothèque interuniversitaire de la Sorbonne in 1939 and reports it fully digitized under an open licence. Papus died in 1916, so the gift passed through his estate or heirs; the intermediate custody could not be established from the record alone. The month is unknown and orders the stop.
stops.campa: A notebook of three hundred and three leaves, on the historical existence of Jesus, enters the Sorbonne's interuniversity library in 1939 as a gift from Papus, who has been dead for twenty-three years. What the manuscript did in the interval nobody has recorded, and the record does not name whose hands it passed through. It is catalogued as MS 1823/5 and has since been digitized in full under an open licence: three hundred and three leaves of his handwriting, readable by anyone who cares to look. What is actually in them has not been reported by anybody writing about him.
suggested_refs: Bibliothèque interuniversitaire de la Sorbonne, MS 1823/5, digitized on NuBIS
